Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Liberia predominantly use paper-based registers and ledgers for recording patient data, such as OPD, ANC, immunization, and inpatient registers (average 21-24 per facility). Data is aggregated monthly onto paper HMIS forms, verified, and submitted to county health teams, where it is entered into DHIS2 for analysis—no digital entry or EMR at the point of service in rural clinics.MEASURE Evaluation PRISM assessment 2014 Isolated digital pilots exist, e.g., OpenMRS EMR rollout by Partners In Health at J.J. Dossen Hospital (rural, Maryland County) in 2020, replacing paper records there, with plans for expansion, but limited to partner-supported sites.Partners In Health Recent sources (2026 FB post) note most facilities still rely on paper records. Key barriers: poor infrastructure (internet/power/connectivity), low staff skills for digital tools, funding shortages, post-Ebola fragility. National ambitions include DHIS2 at county level and digital transformation plans (e.g., 2022-2027 agenda), but rural point-of-care remains paper-based with digital only for aggregate reporting—wide gap between policy and rural reality.

revision_notes: Verified operational digital pilots at rural clinics: Partners In Health's OpenMRS EMR at J.J. Dossen Hospital (rural Maryland County, since July 2020), and a DHIS2 Tracker for HIV client records at 21 PEPFAR-supported facilities (since 2021) covering 70% of PLHIV nationally, both of which replaced paper registers at those sites. This is more than isolated/negligible digital use, so "entirely paper" understates the position. At the same time, the vast majority of rural clinics remain paper-only, confirmed by the Ministry of Health's May 2026 nationwide EMR Readiness Assessment, launched precisely because facility-level EMR deployment does not yet exist at scale. Recalculated to code 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). Not a top-of-scale change.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Liberia remain predominantly paper-based, using ledger registers for OPD, ANC, immunisation and inpatient records that are later aggregated into DHIS2 at county level. Isolated but operational digital pilots exist at facility level, including Partners In Health's OpenMRS electronic medical records system at J.J. Dossen Hospital in rural Maryland County (rolled out in 2020) and a DHIS2 Tracker system for HIV client-level data introduced at 21 high-volume facilities from 2021, which replaced paper registers for that programme. In May 2026 the Ministry of Health, through the National Health Intelligence Center, launched a nationwide Connected Facilities Assessment to gauge readiness for a broader rollout of electronic medical records, underlining that routine digital data capture is not yet the norm in rural facilities. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, limited staff digital skills, and funding constraints.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural police stations in Liberia record criminal cases and complaints using paper files and dockets. A January 2026 report on Nyehn Town Police Station in rural Todee District describes no computers available; officers prioritize protecting paper documents from rain over duties, indicating entirely manual processes amid dilapidated infrastructure lacking basic logistics.FrontPageAfrica An EGAP study on rural community policing (2010s) notes historically low formal reporting (2% of crimes to police), relying on administrative data without digital mention.EGAP Digital systems exist at national/urban levels: UNDP-supported CSIS (2021, Montserrado urban pilot) uses tablets for biodata/GPS input and online aggregation, replacing paper stats reporting.UNDP CSIS CMIS/DHIS2 (2022 rollout to police) offers offline mobile app for case stats with GPS, improving data integrity, but no evidence of routine rural point-of-service use; training focused on county-level staff.UNDP CMIS Barriers: poor infrastructure/electricity, low connectivity, training gaps, resource scarcity in rural areas. National digital ambitions (UNDP pilots) contrast sharply with rural paper reality; systems likely for aggregate reporting post-paper collection. Score 1: entirely paper at rural facilities; digital limited to urban pilots.

revision_notes: Confirmed. January 2026 reporting on the Nyehn Town Police Station in rural Todee District explicitly notes the absence of computers and continued reliance on paper case files, corroborating the original code of 1 (entirely paper). UNDP-supported digital case management pilots (CSIS since 2021, CMIS since 2022) are concentrated in Montserrado County and at county-level training, with no evidence of routine digital data capture at rural stations. revised_comments: Rural police stations in Liberia record cases, complaints and crime statistics almost entirely on paper. A January 2026 report on the Nyehn Town Police Station in rural Todee District, Lower Montserrado County, describes a dilapidated facility with no computers available, where officers prioritise protecting paper case files from rain damage over other duties. UNDP-supported digital case management tools - an online Case Management Information System for justice institutions and a Crime Statistics Information System using tablets with GPS-tagged reporting - have been piloted since 2021-2022, but rollout has concentrated on Montserrado County and county-level training rather than routine use at rural stations. Persistent barriers include poor infrastructure, unreliable electricity and connectivity, and limited resources in rural areas.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Liberia predominantly use paper-based registers for daily administrative data, attendance, and learning records. National EMIS transitioned from paper-based 1.0 to planned digital 2.0, but data collection stalled post-2022 census due to funding shortages; no new school census data since.Liberia EMIS Peer Review Report Weak ICT infrastructure (limited hardware, high internet costs, unreliable electricity) severely limits point-of-service digital use in rural areas.Liberia EMIS Peer Review Report Recent initiatives include Mar 2026 Geo-Mapping M&E system for real-time monitoring (attendance, instruction) with geolocated inputs from schools (pilot incl. some rural counties like Rivercess, Bong), and planned mobile/SMS/ODK tools for low-connectivity.FrontPageAfrica Rural network expansion (128 sites covering 100+ schools by 2024) improves access but insufficient for routine digital recording.ZTE Report Barriers: funding dependency, staff capacity, utilities/transport. National ambition for EMIS 2.0 contrasts with rural paper reality; pilots indicate score 2, no evidence of majority digital at rural POSC.

revision_notes: The original Value Code of 1 (entirely paper) was inconsistent with the row's own Comments, which concluded pilots "indicate score 2". Fresh evidence confirms code 2 is correct: the Ministry of Education's Geo-Mapping Monitoring and Evaluation System, launched March 2026 and piloted in five counties including rural Rivercess, Sinoe, Bomi and Gbarpolu, had schools input real-time, geo-referenced monitoring data directly on-site; June 2026 reporting confirms this pilot phase concluded with "encouraging results" and contributed to a rise in accredited schools nationwide. This is verified, operational point-of-service digital data capture in a meaningful subset of rural schools, alongside continued predominant reliance on paper elsewhere (per the September 2025 EMIS Peer Review Report noting stalled EMIS 2.0 rollout and weak ICT infrastructure). Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital); not a top-of-scale change.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Liberia predominantly rely on paper-based registers for attendance, enrolment and administrative records, reflecting a national Education Management Information System still transitioning from a paper-based EMIS 1.0 to a digitised EMIS 2.0, hampered by funding shortfalls and weak ICT infrastructure. Some point-of-service digital data capture has now been demonstrated in rural areas, however: the Ministry of Education's Geo-Mapping Monitoring and Evaluation System, launched in March 2026 with a US$300,000 government investment, had school staff enter real-time, geo-referenced monitoring data directly on-site during its pilot phase across five counties, including rural Rivercess, Sinoe, Bomi and Gbarpolu. By June 2026 the pilot had concluded with positive results, feeding into a broader school accreditation and monitoring drive. A parallel 2025/2026 Annual School Census also introduced greater use of school-based data collection and digital validation, though this remains centred on County Data Hubs rather than direct facility-level digital entry. Overall, rural schools remain mostly paper-based with a growing but still limited degree of digital data capture.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices and civil registration points in Liberia predominantly use paper-based forms for birth registrations. The 15 county-level registration centers are located in urban districts, serving rural households located 5-10 km away (often requiring 5+ hours travel by foot). Completeness remains low at <25% as of 2018.UNECA CRVS Snapshot No computers in local registration or health facilities; paper records are standard, with data potentially aggregated digitally at county centers. Digital initiatives are limited to pilots and donor projects: The Mobile Birth Registration (MBR) pilot (2009-2012) used Nokia phones for data collection by district health officers in one rural county (Bomi), supplementing paper processes to enable certificate printing; it demonstrated feasibility but faced scale-up barriers and remained isolated.VTT ReportWHO eCRVS Review Recent UNICEF efforts (2024) integrate birth registration in 98% health districts using tablets/online systems linked to DHIS2 for digital certificates, but challenges like unreliable electricity, internet, resources, and decentralized accountability persist, indicating non-standardized use.FrontPageAfrica/UNICEF Key barriers: poor infrastructure/power, low capacity, post-conflict fragility. National plans (2016-2020) envision expansion and online rollout, but rural point-of-service remains paper-default with digital only in isolated health-linked pilots—not majority routine use. Score 2 fits: predominantly paper with some digital pilots.

revision_notes: Confirmed at 2 (Mostly paper - some digital), superseding the older 2011 mobile-registration pilot and 2018/2019 UNECA snapshot cited previously. UNICEF's December 2024 statement describes decentralisation of birth registration to all 15 counties and 98% of health districts, with tablets and an online registration system used for issuing digital birth certificates - a materially more advanced digital footprint than the earlier isolated pilots. However, an April 2026 CENTAL "Service-on-the-Wheel" mobile registration drive in rural Bong County reported technical difficulties limiting on-the-spot digital certificate printing, and standard process descriptions (World Bank ID4D) still show paper birth notification forms as the entry point, with data entered into an electronic database at a later stage rather than always at first point of contact. This mixed evidence supports "mostly paper - some digital" rather than a higher code.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry services in Liberia operate through a decentralised network of county-level registration centres and health-facility-linked registration points, with birth notification typically first recorded on paper before being entered into a central electronic database. Digitalisation has advanced since earlier isolated pilots: as of December 2024, UNICEF reported that birth registration had been decentralised to all 15 counties, reaching 98% of health districts, with tablets and an online registration system used to issue digital birth certificates, and records integrated into the DHIS2 platform for real-time reporting. In practice, however, digital delivery in rural areas remains uneven; an April 2026 mobile "Service-on-the-Wheel" registration drive in rural Bong County registered 477 children but encountered technical difficulties that delayed printing of digital certificates for many of them. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet connectivity, and rural households often remain several hours' travel from a registration point. Overall, rural civil registry offices are best characterised as mostly paper-based with a growing but still partial degree of digital data capture.
